newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe says spending cap needed for euro.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe says spending cap needed for euro.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Sunday that France needed to take further savings measures to meet the criteria for a single European currency and accused the left-wing opposition of being totally divided on Europe.

Juppe said it was up to President Jacques Chirac to name a prime minister if his centre-right coalition wins a snap parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, and insisted he was not campaigning to keep his own job.

Voters had the choice between re-electing the coalition that would govern in harmony with Chirac or plunging into another period of "cohabitation" with a left-wing alliance which "would be bound to drag France a bit further down".

"I'm absolutely not a candidate for my own succession," Juppe told TF1 television in a prime-time interview. "It would be very arrogant and insolent to say 'it's me'. It's absurd. It is the president who decides."
He said the government would cap public spending in real terms for five years to reduce deficits and unemployment if it wins the election, as opinion polls predict.

Asked whether a further dose of austerity was needed for France to meet the Maastricht Treaty's public deficit limit of three percent of gross domestic product, he said: "We are within forecast, and everyone agrees we are not far off."

"It is true that a little extra effort may be necessary. Of course I am not going to deny that. That's why I say we cannot increase public spending," Juppe said. He also ruled out increasing taxes, saying Chirac had made that a solemn pledge.

If re-elected, the coalition would implement a series of immediate measures within 40 days, setting a five-year plan for expenditure and revenue to ensure that public spending did not increase in real terms, Juppe said.

Asked if he advocated a five-year freeze on spending at current nominal levels, he said: "That would not be realistic. I said it (expenditure) must not increase from one year to the next in real terms. Later, spending must rise less than inflation so it does not eat into the national wealth."
Juppe said the coalition planned to continue reducing the civil service for the next two or three years by not replacing about 5,000 of the 60,000 public servants who retired each year.
With growth forecast at three percent next year, France would have room to cut taxes beyond what had been done so far and to reduce deficits further, he said.
Juppe wrote to cabinet ministers last week ordering them to hold 1998 spending at the same level as 1997 and 1996 in nominal terms, a cut of almost two percent in real terms.
The prime minister's statement that he was not fighting for his own job seemed aimed at deflecting attacks by the Socialist and Communist opposition, which has made him a central target.

Opinion polls in late 1996 showed that Juppe, 51, was the least popular prime minister since the start of the Fifth Republic in 1958, blamed for record unemployment and austerity to help France qualify for a single European currency.
"My only ambition is to help to win this campaign because I believe it is in the interest of France" for the centre-right coalition to keep its National Assembly majority, he said.

He said Chirac could choose a premier from a wide range of conservative politicians. "What I've done in the past two years has not been easy. There were moments of great tension, it's taken courage...And the results show progress," he said.
The premier did not rule out a face-to-face television debate with Socialist leader Lionel Jospin between the two rounds of voting.
